title: Follow the Yellow Brick Road. Then What?
author: Kristen McQuillan
summary: Kristen McQuillan uses the Wizard of Oz as a frame for the stage of literacy reform that comes after curriculum adoption. Her worry is that districts have spent years choosing better materials and are now entering the field of poppies, where implementation work gets tedious and attention drifts. She argues that adoption is not implementation, and she uses the Lippitt-Knoster model of vision, skills, incentives, resources and an action plan to diagnose what is missing when a good curriculum does not show up in classrooms. Her central move is to measure implementation itself, rather than waiting on lagging achievement data, by regularly sampling classrooms with a few consistent indicators. She suggests two questions: are teachers using the materials, and how well are they using them. The payoff is that leaders can stop guessing and target support at one specific instructional challenge, then return and look again in a continuous improvement cycle.
points: Adopting a high-quality curriculum is only the start, because a clear vision, teacher skill, incentives, resources and an action plan must all be present for change to hold.
Student achievement data lags behind instruction, so leaders also need a measure of whether the intended instructional changes actually occurred.
A sample of classroom visits against two questions, whether teachers use the materials and how well, separates a usage problem from a quality problem.
Observations should narrow the next step to a bite-sized priority, such as teachers rushing the knowledge and vocabulary portions of lessons, rather than launching another broad PD initiative.
An implementation action plan should be a learning process of observe, learn, prioritize, support and repeat, not just a list of activities to complete.
quotes: But assessment results are largely lagging indicators. They tell us something about the outcomes of instruction, not necessarily whether the instructional changes we intended to make actually occurred.
The problem isn’t necessarily that districts have chosen the wrong reforms. It’s that they often don’t know enough about how those reforms are unfolding.

This isn’t about policing teachers or demanding mindless compliance. It’s about understanding whether the system’s intended instructional approach is actually reaching students—and identifying what’s getting in the way when it isn’t.
School systems can be clear about what they want to accomplish and still have an enormous amount to learn about how to accomplish it.
The goal is to get a little smarter about it every time we look. And the looking is as important as the doing.
But following the Yellow Brick Road isn’t the same thing as reaching the Emerald City.
There’s an important measurement step between adoption and achievement. And that step is measuring implementation itself.
